content: " * This article discusses how author Jeffrey Eugenides believes that personal shame and national shame in America are deeply connected—just as people feel guilt about their own choices or past, the country also carries guilt from its history, like slavery. He suggests you can’t really separate the two because a nation is simply made up of individuals. In 2005, before major national events like Hurricane Katrina or the election of Donald Trump, Eugenides already felt America had a lot to be ashamed of. Now, over a decade later, those feelings seem even stronger. He talks about this while sitting in a new library at Princeton University, where he teaches. The unfinished building—marked only with a hand-written “unisex” sign—highlights how much social norms, especially around identity and inclusion, have shifted. Back when his Pulitzer Prize–winning novel Middlesex came out, many readers didn’t even know what “intersex” meant, showing how awareness has grown since. This change creates both tension and progress on campuses and beyond. Eugenides’ short story “Great Experiment” captures this mix of sadness and irony about American life. The quote about shame being endless in both personal and national ways shows how hard it is to move forward without reckoning with the past. People today often wrestle with how to act ethically in a fractured society, whether discussing politics with a girlfriend or just walking down the street. That inner struggle reflects larger national issues. Even something as simple as using a restroom has become a symbol of deeper cultural debates. Despite the heaviness, there’s also a welcome sense of honesty in facing these truths. * Eugenides’ reflections serve as a highlight of how literature can help process collective feelings during uncertain times. He doesn’t offer easy answers but encourages awareness of both personal flaws and national injustices. This duality affects everything—from intimate relationships to public health conversations. The tension between wanting to belong and feeling disappointed in your country is something many feel deeply. Still, acknowledging these shared struggles can be a first step toward healing. His sadness, mixed with humor, shows he hasn’t given up on America or its people. Instead, he sees value in examining both individual lives and the broader national story with compassion. That kind of reflection might even improve how we treat a girlfriend or neighbor during divisive times. At its core, his message is that progress starts with honesty about where we’ve been and who we are. And maybe, just maybe, that honesty creates a more inclusive and welcome future for everyone."
